name: Chapter 19: Chemical Coordination and Integration
description: Endocrine glands and their hormones, disorders, hormones of heart, kidney and gut, and mechanism of hormone action

cards.definition: Neural: fast but short-lived, point-to-point. Hormonal: slower, longer lasting, reaches cells nerves do not innervate.

cards.term: Why are endocrine glands called ductless?
cards.definition: They lack ducts; secretions go into the blood
Exocrine: secretes through ducts (e.g. salivary). Endocrine: ductless, secretes hormones into blood.
Non-nutrient chemicals that act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts

cards.term: Why was the hormone definition broadened?
cards.definition: To include many new molecules made outside the organised endocrine glands (e.g. by the gut, heart, kidney)

cards.term: Organised endocrine glands of the human body?
cards.definition: Pituitary, pineal, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, parathyroid, thymus, gonads (testis, ovary)

cards.term: Other organs that also produce hormones?
cards.definition: Gastrointestinal tract, liver, kidney, heart
Basal part of the diencephalon (forebrain)
Groups of neurosecretory cells that produce hormones
Releasing (stimulate pituitary secretion) and inhibiting (inhibit it)
GnRH: stimulates pituitary release of gonadotrophins
Somatostatin: inhibits release of growth hormone

cards.term: How do hypothalamic hormones reach the anterior pituitary?
cards.definition: Through a portal circulatory system

cards.term: How does the hypothalamus control the posterior pituitary?
cards.definition: By direct neural regulation
In a bony cavity, the sella turcica, attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints "sella tursica". Correct spelling?
cards.definition: Sella turcica ("Turkish saddle")

cards.term: Two anatomical parts of the pituitary?
cards.definition: Adenohypophysis (pars distalis + pars intermedia) and neurohypophysis (pars nervosa)

cards.term: Six hormones of the pars distalis (anterior pituitary)?
cards.definition: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH
"FLAT PiG": FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, Prolactin, GH
MSH (melanocyte stimulating hormone); in humans the pars intermedia is almost merged with the pars distalis

cards.term: Hormones released by the posterior pituitary?
cards.definition: Oxytocin and vasopressin. They are made in the hypothalamus and transported axonally; the neurohypophysis only stores and releases them.
Excess GH in childhood: Gigantism; Low GH in childhood: Pituitary dwarfism; Excess GH in adults (middle age): Acromegaly (face disfigured)

cards.definition: Hard to diagnose early; goes undetected for years; can cause serious complications and premature death
Growth of mammary glands and milk formation
Stimulates synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormones
Stimulates glucocorticoid secretion from the adrenal cortex

cards.term: Why are LH and FSH called gonadotrophins?
cards.definition: They stimulate gonadal activity
LH: androgen secretion from testis. FSH + androgens: regulate spermatogenesis.
LH: induces ovulation of the Graafian follicle and maintains the corpus luteum. FSH: growth of ovarian follicles.
Acts on melanocytes: regulates skin pigmentation
Contraction of smooth muscle: vigorous uterine contraction at childbirth and milk ejection

cards.term: Function of vasopressin, and its other name?
cards.definition: Water and electrolyte reabsorption by the distal tubules, reducing water loss; ADH (antidiuretic hormone)
Impaired synthesis or release of ADH → kidneys cannot conserve water → water loss, dehydration
Insipidus: ADH problem, dilute urine, no sugar. Mellitus: insulin problem, glucose in urine.
Hypothalamic hormones: Pituitary; TSH (thyrotrophin): Thyroid; ACTH (corticotrophin): Adrenal cortex; LH, FSH (gonadotrophins): Gonads; MSH (melanotrophin): Melanocytes (skin)

cards.definition: Dorsal side of the forebrain
Melatonin
Regulates 24-hour (diurnal) rhythms: sleep-wake cycle, body temperature; also metabolism, pigmentation, menstrual cycle, defence

cards.term: Why is melatonin secreted mainly at night? (intuition)
cards.definition: Light inhibits it; darkness raises it, signalling the body that it is night (why screens late at night disturb sleep)
Two lobes on either side of the trachea, joined by a thin flap, the isthmus

cards.term: What makes up the thyroid gland?
cards.definition: Follicles (follicular cells around a cavity) and stromal tissue

cards.term: Two thyroid hormones from follicular cells?
cards.definition: Thyroxine (T₄) and triiodothyronine (T₃)

cards.term: Which element is essential for thyroid hormones?
cards.definition: Iodine
Hypothyroidism and thyroid enlargement: goitre
Hypothyroidism during pregnancy: stunted growth, intellectual disability, low IQ, abnormal skin, deaf-mutism in the baby

cards.term: Effect of hypothyroidism in adult women?
cards.definition: Irregular menstrual cycle
Thyroid cancer or nodules
Hyperthyroidism with enlarged thyroid, protruding eyeballs, raised BMR, weight loss
Regulate basal metabolic rate; support RBC formation; control carbohydrate, protein, fat metabolism; water and electrolyte balance
A protein hormone from the thyroid that lowers blood calcium

cards.term: Correction: NCERT spells it "Exopthalmic goitre". Correct?
cards.definition: Exophthalmic (Greek ophthalmos = eye)

cards.term: Number and location of parathyroid glands?
cards.definition: Four, on the back side of the thyroid (one pair in each lobe)

cards.term: Hormone of the parathyroid, and what regulates it?
cards.definition: Parathyroid hormone (PTH), a peptide; regulated by circulating Ca²⁺ levels
Stimulates bone resorption (demineralisation); Ca²⁺ reabsorption by renal tubules; Ca²⁺ absorption from digested food
It increases blood Ca²⁺
PTH raises blood Ca²⁺; TCT lowers it: together they balance calcium

cards.term: What happens if the parathyroids are removed? (link to Ch 17)
cards.definition: Blood Ca²⁺ falls → tetany (muscle spasms)
Between the lungs, behind the sternum, on the ventral side of the aorta
Thymosins (peptides)
Differentiation of T-lymphocytes (cell-mediated immunity); promote antibody production (humoral immunity)

cards.term: Why are immune responses weaker in old people?
cards.definition: The thymus degenerates with age, so thymosin production falls

cards.term: Location and parts of the adrenal gland?
cards.definition: One above each kidney; central medulla, outer cortex
Adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline (norepinephrine): catecholamines

cards.term: Why are catecholamines called emergency (fight or flight) hormones?
cards.definition: They are secreted rapidly in stress and emergencies
Alertness, pupil dilation, piloerection, sweating; faster, stronger heartbeat; faster breathing; glycogen breakdown (↑ blood glucose); breakdown of lipids and proteins

cards.text: Adrenal cortex layers from inside out: {{c1::zona reticularis}} → {{c2::zona fasciculata}} → {{c3::zona glomerulosa}}.

cards.term: Mnemonic for adrenal cortex layers (outside in) and products?
cards.definition: "GFR": Glomerulosa (salt: aldosterone), Fasciculata (sugar: cortisol), Reticularis (sex: androgens). "Salt, sugar, sex."
Glucocorticoids (main: cortisol): carbohydrate metabolism. Mineralocorticoids (main: aldosterone): water and electrolyte balance.
Gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, proteolysis; inhibit amino acid uptake; maintain heart and kidney function; anti-inflammatory, suppress immunity; stimulate RBC production
At renal tubules: reabsorbs Na⁺ and water, excretes K⁺ and phosphate → maintains electrolytes, fluid volume, osmotic pressure, BP
Growth of axial, pubic and facial hair at puberty
Underproduction of adrenal cortex hormones → altered carbohydrate metabolism, acute weakness and fatigue

cards.term: Why is the pancreas a composite gland?
cards.definition: It is both exocrine and endocrine

cards.term: Endocrine part of the pancreas, with numbers?
cards.definition: Islets of Langerhans: 1–2 million, only 1–2% of pancreatic tissue
On liver: glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; reduces cellular glucose uptake → hyperglycemia
On hepatocytes and adipocytes: ↑ glucose uptake and use, glycogenesis → hypoglycemia
Hyperglycemic: glucagon (also adrenaline, cortisol). Hypoglycemic: insulin.
Prolonged hyperglycemia from insulin deficiency and/or resistance: glucose in urine, harmful ketone bodies; treated with insulin therapy
Alpha → glucagon ("Adds" sugar to blood); Beta → insulin ("Brings it down")

cards.term: Where are the testes, and what are their two roles?
cards.definition: In the scrotal sac outside the abdomen; primary sex organ and endocrine gland

cards.term: Which cells of the testis make androgens?
cards.definition: Leydig (interstitial) cells in the intertubular spaces; mainly testosterone
Development of male accessory organs; muscular growth, facial and axillary hair, low voice, aggressiveness; spermatogenesis; libido; anabolic effects
Estrogen and progesterone (steroids)
Estrogen: growing ovarian follicles. Progesterone: corpus luteum (after ovulation).
Growth of female secondary sex organs, follicle development, female secondary sex characters (high-pitched voice), mammary development, sexual behaviour
Supports pregnancy; forms mammary alveoli and milk secretion
Progesterone

cards.term: What is ANF, and what does it do?
cards.definition: Atrial natriuretic factor from the atrial wall; dilates vessels to lower blood pressure
ANF

cards.term: Hormone of the kidney, and its role?
cards.definition: Erythropoietin (from JG cells): stimulates RBC formation
Gastrin: Gastric glands: HCl and pepsinogen; Secretin: Exocrine pancreas: water and HCO₃⁻; Cholecystokinin (CCK): Pancreatic enzymes and bile; GIP: Inhibits gastric secretion and motility

cards.definition: Hormones from non-endocrine tissues, essential for normal growth, repair and regeneration

cards.term: How do hormones act on target tissues?
cards.definition: By binding to specific hormone receptors present only in target tissues
Membrane-bound: on the cell membrane. Intracellular: inside the cell, mostly nuclear.
Each receptor binds one hormone only

Peptide/protein: Insulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones; Steroids: Cortisol, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone; Iodothyronines: Thyroid hormones; Amino-acid derivatives: Epinephrine

advancedHtml.backHtml:

Examples?

Peptide/proteinInsulin, glucagon, pituitary and hypothalamic hormones
SteroidsCortisol, testosterone, estradiol, progesterone

cards.term: How do hormones with membrane receptors act?
cards.definition: They do not enter the cell; they generate second messengers (cAMP, IP₃, Ca²⁺) that regulate metabolism
FSH binds a membrane receptor on ovarian cells → second messenger (cAMP) → biochemical responses → ovarian growth

cards.term: How do steroid and thyroid hormones act?
cards.definition: Enter the cell, bind intracellular receptors; the complex acts on the genome to regulate gene expression

cards.term: Why can steroid hormones enter cells? (intuition)
cards.definition: They are lipid-soluble and pass through the lipid membrane; peptides are water-soluble and cannot
T₄: Thyroid; PTH: Parathyroid; GnRH: Hypothalamus; LH: Pituitary
